AI4MOBILITY · GENERATIVE MODELS IN TRANSPORTATION

Thirty-four papers on generative models in transportation, and what each one generates

Each card shows one paper’s key figure, answers the same five questions in plain words (what it generates, from what, with which model, how the output is steered, and what it is used for), and marks which of the three moves it makes: sample, steer, or fill in. The papers are grouped by eight transportation problems, the same ones the course handout Generative Models in Transportation is built on. At the end: what the papers share, which model family fits which job, and how the field moved.

Reading the small diagram on each card
  • Sample: draw new data that looks like the training data (more of the same).
  • Steer: draw data that meets a condition or leans toward a goal (conditioning, guidance, searching a latent space).
  • Fill in: keep what was observed and generate only the missing part (gap filling, inpainting, one sensor from another).
  • Filled boxes are the moves the paper makes; dashed boxes are moves it does not. The sand bar names the model family.

Filter by transportation problem or by model family, or jump to a year. A paper can belong to more than one family.

1 · Several possible futures

Draw several plausible futures for pedestrians and vehicles instead of one average path.

Social GAN

Gupta et al. · CVPR 2018 · paper · [P14]
Several possible futuresGAN
Generates
Several possible future paths for every pedestrian in a crowd, as (x, y) points every 0.4 s, 3.2 s or 4.8 s ahead.
Conditioned on
Each person's last 3.2 s of positions (8 points) plus a pooled summary of everyone else's relative positions and motion in the scene.
Model
Conditional GAN. The generator is an LSTM encoder–decoder that takes the past plus random noise z; the discriminator is an LSTM that judges whether past plus future looks real.
Steered by
Nothing beyond the conditions: it samples. A 'variety loss' in training penalizes only the best of k samples, so samples spread over different plausible futures.
Used for
Forecasting pedestrian motion for self-driving cars and social robots that move through crowds.

Social GAN predicts where pedestrians will walk, trained on the ETH and UCY crowd datasets (1536 pedestrians in 4 scenes). The generator reads each person's recent track with an LSTM, pools information about every other person (their relative positions go through a small network, then a max-pool), adds random noise, and decodes a future path. The discriminator sees the whole track and learns to flag socially odd ones, such as walking into someone. New noise gives a different future. Idea to remember: the variety loss scores only the best of k samples, which pushes the generator to cover several futures instead of one average path.

What they found
  • One GAN sample was less accurate than a plain LSTM (average ADE 0.49/0.74 m vs 0.43/0.70 m at 3.2/4.8 s), but the best of 20 samples with the variety loss reached 0.39/0.58 m (Table 1).
  • Training with the variety loss beat simply drawing more samples from a model trained without it: on average 33% better with k = 100 (Figure 4).

For mobility: Simulate many plausible pedestrian responses at a crosswalk or station platform to test signal timing or AV yielding logic against a spread of behaviors, not one average walker.

Watch out: Best-of-20 scoring credits the model if any one of 20 samples is close, which flatters samplers; the model also sees only other people, not curbs, walls or vehicles.

Trajectron++

Salzmann, Ivanovic, Chakravarty & Pavone · ECCV 2020 · paper · [P01]
Several possible futuresVAE
Generates
Several possible future (x, y) paths for every pedestrian and vehicle in the scene: 4.8 s ahead on the ETH/UCY pedestrian data, up to 4 s on nuScenes.
Conditioned on
Each agent's past positions and velocities, nearby road users (linked in a graph by distance), a local semantic map patch, and optionally the autonomous vehicle's own planned path.
Model
A conditional VAE with 25 discrete latent behavior modes. LSTM encoders feed a GRU decoder that outputs accelerations and steering rates, which a simple vehicle model integrates into positions.
Steered by
Optionally the ego vehicle's planned path, to ask what others would do if it drives that way; otherwise nothing beyond the conditions: it samples.
Used for
Motion planning and decision-making for autonomous vehicles and robots that share space with pedestrians and other vehicles.

Trajectron++ draws the scene as a graph: each road user is a node, and an edge links two users close enough to influence each other. Recurrent encoders (LSTMs) summarize each agent's past track, its neighbors, and a map patch around it. A conditional VAE then picks one of 25 latent behavior modes (for example, turn right or go straight), and the decoder outputs controls, acceleration and steering rate, that a simple vehicle model (no sliding sideways) integrates into positions. Sampling many modes and controls gives a spread of futures. Idea to remember: generate controls rather than positions, so every sampled path is one a vehicle could physically drive.

What they found
  • Averaged over five pedestrian scenes, the negative log-likelihood of the real path under 2000 samples (lower is better) was −1.14 for Trajectron++ with dynamics vs 5.80 for Social GAN and 1.79 for Trajectron (Table 3).
  • With the map input, 1.0% of sampled pedestrian paths ran into obstacles on the ETH-University scene, compared with 4.6% without the map (Section 5.1).

For mobility: Sample many physically drivable futures for each pedestrian and vehicle at a crosswalk or intersection to estimate how often conflicts could arise, instead of trusting one most-likely path.

Watch out: Predictions are short-range (trained to 3 s on nuScenes) and use a simplified vehicle model, so they say little about rare, long-horizon maneuvers or exact vehicle physics.

MotionLM

Seff et al. · ICCV 2023 · paper · [P16]
Several possible futuresToken model
Generates
Joint futures for interacting agents as sequences of discrete motion tokens, one (Δx, Δy) step every 0.5 s for 8 s, sampled many times (512 rollouts per model copy).
Conditioned on
Road graph, traffic light states and recent histories of surrounding agents, read by a Wayformer early-fusion encoder; optionally a fixed future for one agent.
Model
Autoregressive transformer decoder trained like a language model to predict the next motion token (169-token vocabulary); it attends to the scene and to all agents' earlier tokens.
Steered by
Conditioning only: fix one agent's actions and roll out the others step by step, so they can react to it; otherwise it simply samples.
Used for
Interaction-aware motion forecasting for self-driving planning, tested on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset interactive challenge.

MotionLM writes traffic as a sentence. Each agent's path is cut into 0.5 s steps, and each step's movement (Δx, Δy) is rounded to one of 169 motion tokens, like words in a vocabulary. A transformer reads the scene, then generates one token per agent per step; every agent's choice depends on what all agents did in earlier steps, so they can yield or pass in response. Sampling hundreds of rollouts gives many joint futures, which are clustered into six weighted modes. Idea to remember: no latent variable or anchor paths are needed; variety comes simply from sampling tokens, as in a language model.

What they found
  • When agents could not attend to each other during the rollout (marginal version), predicted overlaps (collisions) were a relative 38% higher than in the joint version (Table 3, validation set).
  • Sampling enough futures matters: 32 rollouts per model copy were already enough to beat the previous top entry on joint mAP (Section 4.5, Fig. 6).

For mobility: Ask what a pedestrian or cross traffic would do if the AV turns now, by fixing one agent's path and rolling out the others, to screen unprotected-turn conflicts.

Watch out: Conditioning can mislead: letting the model see one agent's whole future scored better yet gave nonsensical 'reactions', and the authors make no claim of true cause and effect.

MotionDiffuser

Jiang et al. · CVPR 2023 · paper · [P15]
Several possible futuresDiffusion
Generates
Joint future paths for all modeled agents at once, 80 (x, y) points each (up to 8 s ahead), as many samples as wanted (64 per agent in the control tests).
Conditioned on
Agent histories, traffic light states and the road graph from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, encoded by a Wayformer transformer into condition tokens.
Model
Conditional diffusion model. A transformer denoiser lets agents' noisy paths attend to each other and to the scene tokens; paths are compressed to 10 PCA components before diffusion.
Steered by
Guidance: the gradient of any differentiable cost is added at each denoising step, e.g., an attractor pulling chosen points to targets or a repeller keeping agents apart.
Used for
Multi-agent motion prediction for self-driving cars, and building tailored simulation scenarios with rules or physical priors enforced.

MotionDiffuser generates the futures of all agents in a scene together, as one joint sample. In training, noise is added to real future paths from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, and a transformer learns to remove it while reading the scene (map, signals, histories). To predict, it starts from pure noise and denoises in 32 steps, giving many joint futures that are clustered into six. Paths are first compressed with PCA; 3 components already explain 99.7% of the variance. With the same scene encoder, the diffusion head beat Wayformer on all metrics. Idea to remember: a cost's gradient, added during denoising, steers samples while keeping them realistic.

What they found
  • With an attractor pulling each path's end toward a target, the mean end-point error (meanSFDE) was 0.747 and minSADE, a realism proxy, 0.533; fixing paths with an optimizer after sampling met targets but looked unrealistic (Table 2, Fig. 6).
  • A repeller cost between agents cut the overlap rate of joint predictions (agents running into each other) to 0.008, which the authors call an order-of-magnitude drop (Table 2).

For mobility: Build what-if test scenarios, such as a car that must end in a given lane, by writing the goal as a cost and guiding a trained motion model.

Watch out: A guided sample shows what you asked for, not how often it happens in real traffic, so do not read guided scenarios as crash or conflict rates.

DiffusionDrive

Liao et al. · CVPR 2025 · paper · [P03]
Several possible futuresDiffusion
Generates
Candidate driving plans for the ego vehicle, 8 waypoints over 4 s, many at once (20 in the main tests), each with a confidence score; the top-scoring plan is used.
Conditioned on
Camera and LiDAR features from a perception module (bird's-eye-view features plus detected agents); on NAVSIM it reuses Transfuser's perception with a ResNet-34 backbone.
Model
Truncated diffusion policy: a transformer diffusion decoder replaces the planner's regression head and denoises noisy copies of 20 anchor paths in 2 steps, refining them in cascaded layers.
Steered by
No cost guidance. Sampling starts from a prior (20 anchor paths clustered from human driving, lightly noised), and a learned confidence score picks the plan to drive.
Used for
End-to-end autonomous driving: turning raw sensor input directly into the vehicle's own plan in real time (45 FPS on an NVIDIA 4090).

DiffusionDrive swaps the one-answer planning head of an end-to-end driving model for a diffusion model that proposes several plans. A plain diffusion head on Transfuser needed 20 denoising steps, and different noise samples collapsed onto nearly the same path. Their fix: cluster human driving into 20 anchor paths, add only a little noise to them in training (a truncated schedule), and learn to denoise back to the real path. At run time, noisy anchors are cleaned in 2 steps while the decoder reads sensor features, and a classifier scores each plan. Idea to remember: start sampling near typical answers, so few steps still give diverse, realistic options.

What they found
  • A plain diffusion head on Transfuser (TransfuserDP) needed 20 denoising steps, ran at 7 FPS, had a mode-diversity score D of only 11%, and raised the driving score PDMS by just 0.6 (Table 2).
  • DiffusionDrive used 2 steps, reached D = 74% and 45 FPS, and scored PDMS 88.1, +4.1 over the regression-head Transfuser (Table 2); PDMS combines collisions, staying on road, time-to-collision, comfort and progress.

For mobility: Seed a generator with typical local maneuvers (anchors clustered from your own driving data) to get fast, diverse candidate plans when testing ADAS features or automated shuttles.

Watch out: NAVSIM is non-reactive: other vehicles replay their logs and do not respond to the plan, so a high PDMS is not proof of safe driving in real traffic.

2 · Trip and OD data

Make trips and OD tables that keep the patterns of real travel but not the travelers.

DiffTraj

Zhu et al. · NeurIPS 2023 · paper · [P10]
Trip and OD dataDiffusion
Generates
Synthetic GPS trajectories: fixed-length sequences of latitude–longitude points, resized to the wanted length, for taxi trips in Chengdu and Xi'an.
Conditioned on
Trip attributes: start and end regions, departure time, distance, travel time, trip length and speed, embedded by a Wide & Deep network.
Model
Diffusion model (500 noise steps) whose denoiser, Traj-UNet, is a 1D-convolution UNet with an attention block, fed the step number and the trip-attribute embedding.
Steered by
Classifier-free guidance: a weight ω mixes conditional and unconditional noise predictions to trade quality against diversity; start and end regions can be fixed.
Used for
Sharing privacy-minded stand-ins for raw GPS traces and feeding downstream tasks such as grid inflow/outflow forecasting.

DiffTraj learns from millions of taxi GPS trips recorded in Chengdu and Xi'an in November 2016, then draws new, synthetic trips. Each trip is resampled to a fixed number of latitude–longitude points, so it becomes a short two-row signal. In training, noise is added to real trips step by step, and a 1D-convolution UNet (Traj-UNet) learns to predict that noise, given the step number and the trip's attributes (regions, departure time, distance, speed). To generate, it starts from pure noise and removes it step by step; skipping steps speeds this up. Idea to remember: once a trip is a fixed-length signal, standard image-style diffusion tools carry over.

What they found
  • Flow-prediction models trained on synthetic trips almost matched those trained on real trips: AGCRN inflow MSE 4.33 with real data vs 4.55 with DiffTraj data (Table 2).
  • Trips from other generators were less useful for the same task: inflow MSE 6.78 (GAN), 6.79 (VAE) and 4.62 (Diffwave) vs 4.50 for DiffTraj (Table 6).

For mobility: An agency could share synthetic GPS trips that keep city-wide travel patterns so analysts can build demand and flow models, after first testing the data for privacy leaks.

Watch out: The paper argues privacy because trips are generated from noise but runs no privacy attack such as membership inference, so synthetic here is not proven private.

DiffODGen

Rong, Ding, Liu & Li · arXiv 2023 · paper · [P24]
Trip and OD dataDiffusion
Generates
A full commuting OD matrix for a new city: which census-tract pairs have any commuters, and how many workers travel between each pair.
Conditioned on
Each region's census demographics (age, gender, income and more) and OpenStreetMap point-of-interest counts, plus the distance between region centroids.
Model
Two cascaded graph diffusion models with graph-transformer denoisers: discrete diffusion first makes the 0/1 flow pattern, then continuous diffusion generates flow volumes on the kept pairs.
Steered by
The new city's regional features condition every OD cell (classifier-free conditional training); no extra guidance. Stage 1's flow pattern masks where stage 2 generates.
Used for
Estimating commuting demand for cities without travel surveys, for urban planning, traffic control and simulation.

DiffODGen drafts a commuting OD matrix for a city that has no travel survey, using only census and map features. It was trained on Cook County (Chicago) LODES 2018 commuting flows and tested on New York City and Seattle, at census-tract level (721 to 1,319 regions). Stage 1 generates the yes/no pattern of which tract pairs exchange commuters, using discrete diffusion that keeps the matrix sparse. Stage 2 generates flow volumes only on those pairs with ordinary diffusion. Both denoisers are graph transformers that also see node statistics such as degree. Idea to remember: generate the whole matrix jointly, so city-wide patterns like sparsity and heavy-tailed flows come out right.

What they found
  • Trained on Cook County and tested on new cities, flow errors (RMSE/NRMSE) were over 3% lower in New York City and 13% lower in Seattle than the best baseline (Table 2).
  • In New York City, 24.9% of real tract pairs have commuters vs 33.0% in DiffODGen's matrix, while the deep regression baselines came out far too sparse or too dense (Figure 4, Table 3).

For mobility: An MPO or city without a recent household travel survey could draft a commuting OD matrix from census and POI data to seed demand models, then check it against counts.

Watch out: It covers only home-to-work commutes in two test cities, and the authors note a plain diffusion model on the raw matrix was hardly comparable to a gravity model.

CoDiffMob

Zhang et al. · WWW 2025 · paper · [P25]
Trip and OD dataDiffusion
Generates
One-day trajectories for synthetic people: a (latitude, longitude) location at each time step, which together add up to city-wide origin–destination (OD) flows.
Conditioned on
Each person's starting (home) location inside the denoiser; the real OD flows and population map enter only through the starting noise, not the network.
Model
A DDIM diffusion model with a 1-D UNet denoiser (convolutions plus attention over time steps), trained the usual way on real trajectories with plain random noise.
Steered by
A noise prior: a rule-based travel model (stay, go home, revisit, explore) picks trips that follow real OD flows; these are turned into noise, added to random noise, and scaled by hourly activity.
Used for
Shareable synthetic mobility data for city planning studies, and extra training data for next-location prediction models (LSTM and Transformer).

With DDIM (a diffusion sampler with no added randomness), each starting noise gives exactly one trajectory, and each move's direction follows the direction in the noise. So CoDiffMob builds a better starting point than pure random noise. A rule-based travel model draws rough daily trips that respect the real OD flows and population. These trips are run backward through DDIM into noise, added to fresh random noise, and scaled up in busy hours. The denoiser, trained on mobile-network location records from Shanghai and Nanchang, turns this noise into trajectories. Idea worth remembering: you can steer a diffusion model, without retraining it, by choosing where its noise starts.

What they found
  • City-wide flow match (CPC, where 1 means identical OD flows): 0.6842 vs 0.3992 for DiffTraj, a similar diffusion model started from plain random noise (Table 1, Fig. 3, Shanghai data).
  • Removing the noise prior drops CPC from 0.6842 to 0.3416 on the Shanghai data, while using the prior without mixing in random noise hurts individual trip statistics (Table 2).

For mobility: A city could release synthetic daily trips that reproduce its OD matrix by seeding a diffusion model with trips from a simple travel model it already trusts.

Watch out: Better flow match cost some diversity, and privacy was checked only with overlap and membership-inference tests, so synthetic trips are not automatically private.

3 · Crashes and near-misses

Push a model of normal driving toward the dangerous moments an automated vehicle must handle.

STRIVE

Rempe et al. · CVPR 2022 · paper · [P17]
Crashes and near-missesVAE
Generates
6 s future paths (position, heading, speed) for all cars and trucks in a real 8 s nuScenes scene, edited so that some vehicle collides with the AV planner.
Conditioned on
2 s of past motion for each vehicle and a rasterized map (drivable area, lanes, dividers); a graph links every vehicle in the scene.
Model
A conditional VAE built from graph neural networks: a learned prior gives each vehicle a latent vector, and a decoder turns latents into accelerations rolled through a kinematic bicycle model.
Steered by
Latent optimization: gradient descent on all vehicles' latent vectors to bring one close to the planner, plus terms that keep latents likely under the prior, near the start, and otherwise collision-free.
Used for
Stress-testing and tuning AV planners: finding crash types (head-on, rear, side), dropping crashes nobody could avoid, and retuning a rule-based planner's settings.

STRIVE trains a VAE-style traffic model on nuScenes, so each vehicle's next 6 s is coded as a latent vector. To build a test, it encodes a real scene and adjusts the latents by gradient descent until some vehicle hits the AV planner. Every change passes through the decoder and a bicycle model, so edited paths still look like driving, and a prior penalty keeps latents plausible. Because the planner's code is hidden, STRIVE fits a copy of the planner's path inside the model to get gradients. A second search checks that the AV could have avoided the crash. Idea worth remembering: search for crashes in latent space, not raw coordinates.

What they found
  • Against the rule-based planner, edited scenes caused collisions in 27.4% of cases vs 1.2% for the unedited real scenes (Table 1).
  • Compared with a baseline that changes one car's acceleration through a bicycle model without the learned prior, STRIVE's adversary left the drivable area less often (10.8% vs 16.5%) and more crashes were avoidable (83.5% vs 73.4%) (Table 2).

For mobility: A safety team could start from recorded drives, search a learned traffic model for plausible crashes, and keep only avoidable ones to test and retune vehicle control logic.

Watch out: It assumes perfect perception and only vehicle–vehicle crashes, and retuning the planner on many crash scenes made it collide more in normal traffic (Table 3).

CTG

Zhong et al. · ICRA 2023 · paper · [P18]
Crashes and near-missesDiffusion
Generates
Each vehicle's future acceleration and turn-rate sequence, rolled out into (x, y, speed, heading) with a unicycle model; re-planned at 2 Hz over 20 s simulations of nuScenes scenes.
Conditioned on
An agent-centered map image and the past states of the vehicle and its neighbors, encoded by a ResNet.
Model
A conditional diffusion model (U-Net of 1-D temporal convolutions, 100 steps) that denoises actions; states always come from rolling the actions through vehicle dynamics, so paths stay drivable.
Steered by
Guidance: at each denoising step the prediction is moved along the gradient of a rule score written in signal temporal logic; then the best of several samples is kept (filtration).
Used for
Realistic, controllable background traffic for AV simulation: speed limits, target speeds, goal waypoints, stop signs, no collisions and no off-road driving.

CTG trains a diffusion model on nuScenes to propose each vehicle's next seconds of speed change and turning, from a local map image and nearby vehicles' recent motion. Actions are turned into positions with a simple vehicle model, so every sample is drivable. At test time, a user writes a rule in signal temporal logic (STL), a formal language for rules over time such as 'always below the speed limit' or 'eventually reach this point'. STL scores how well a path meets the rule, and the score's gradient nudges the path at every denoising step. Idea worth remembering: train once on real driving, add new rules only at sampling time.

What they found
  • Speed-limit rule: guided CTG scored a violation of 0.019 vs 1.380 for the same model sampled without guidance or filtering, and realism also improved (0.359 vs 0.396; lower is better) (Table II).
  • Combined rule 'stop at the stop sign and stay on the road': stop-sign violation 0.528 vs 2.573 unguided and 0.849 for the best baseline, TrafficSim with optimization (Table III).

For mobility: A simulation team could write local rules (speed limits, stop signs, target speeds) as formulas and get realistic, rule-following background traffic without retraining the model.

Watch out: Rules and realism pull against each other: more guidance steps cut violations but worsen realism and failure rates, and only vehicles were modeled, not pedestrians or cyclists.

TrafficGen

Feng et al. · ICRA 2023 · paper · [P04]
Crashes and near-missesToken model
Generates
A traffic snapshot (each vehicle's position, heading, speed and size) on a real HD map, then each vehicle's long trajectory.
Conditioned on
The HD map split into 5 m lane regions, with lane type and traffic-light state, plus any vehicles already in the scene when adding cars or extending paths.
Model
Autoregressive encoder–decoder: the decoder picks a region from a learned probability map, draws the vehicle's attributes from Gaussian mixtures, re-encodes the scene and repeats; a motion-forecasting head gives trajectories.
Steered by
Nothing beyond the conditions: it samples. The user picks the map, how many vehicles to place, and which real vehicles or trajectory pieces to keep.
Used for
New, denser or completed Waymo scenarios imported into the MetaDrive simulator to test and train a reinforcement-learning driving agent.

Trained on 50,000 Waymo scenes, TrafficGen splits the HD map into 5 m lane regions and encodes the map and existing cars together. Its decoder fills the road one car at a time: pick a region by probability, draw the car's position, heading, speed and size, re-encode, repeat. Each car's long path comes from repeated short forecasts, keeping only the first steps each time. Training hides some cars and asks the model to restore them, like BERT, so it can also add cars to real scenes or extend cut-off paths. Idea worth remembering: build a scene one car at a time, each conditioned on the cars already there.

What they found
  • Placed vehicles match real scenes more closely than with SceneGen: position MMD 0.1192 vs 0.1452 (a distance between distributions; lower is better) (Table I).
  • A reinforcement-learning driving agent trained on denser TrafficGen scenes averaged 2.14 collisions per test episode vs 3.65 when trained on real Waymo scenes, with similar success (0.61 vs 0.60) (Table IV).

For mobility: An agency or AV tester could grow a few recorded intersections into many complete, denser traffic scenes for simulation, without hand-writing rules for where vehicles appear.

Watch out: The scenes are realistic, not deliberately dangerous; realism is judged on distributions of position, heading, speed and size, and safety gains were shown only in the MetaDrive simulator.

LCTGen

Tan et al. · CoRL 2023 · paper · [P12]
Crashes and near-missesLLM
Generates
A 5-second traffic scene on a real Waymo map: each vehicle's start position, heading, speed and size, plus its future path (x, y, heading).
Conditioned on
A plain-English description, such as an NHTSA crash narrative. GPT-4 turns it into a small integer code: lane counts, distance to an intersection, and each car's rough position, direction, speed and action.
Model
GPT-4 is only the reader. A trained transformer Generator outputs probability distributions (Gaussian mixtures for car attributes, 12 path options per car), and the scene is sampled from them.
Steered by
Conditioning only: the code chooses a matching map from 68K Waymo map regions and is fed to the Generator. There is no guidance step and no optimization.
Used for
Building test scenes for self-driving planners from text, including crash reports, and editing real scenes by instruction (e.g., 'make the car in front turn left').

LCTGen turns a sentence into a traffic scene in three steps. GPT-4 reads the text and writes a compact code: lane counts, distance to an intersection, and each car's rough position, direction, speed and action. That code picks a matching road from 68K Waymo map regions, and a transformer Generator places each car on a lane and samples its 5-second path. The Generator never sees text; it learns from real scenes whose codes are computed by fixed rules. Remember that shared code: it lets an LLM steer a traffic model without any paired text-and-scene data.

What they found
  • On 38 NHTSA crash reports, 12 human raters preferred LCTGen's scene over that of MotionCLIP, a text-to-motion baseline, 95.29% of the time (Table 2).
  • When rebuilding Waymo test scenes from their codes, LCTGen's path error (mADE, the average gap between generated and real paths) was 1.329, against 6.683 for MotionCLIP and 10.448 for TrafficGen (Table 1, lower is better).

For mobility: A safety analyst could turn police crash narratives into editable simulation scenes and test how a self-driving planner handles the same conflict.

Watch out: GPT-4 reduces the text to coarse bins (20 m distance, 2.5 m/s speed) and cannot see lane detail, so car placements only roughly match the report.

CTG++

Zhong et al. · CoRL 2023 · paper · [P19]
Crashes and near-missesDiffusionLLM
Generates
Future action and state trajectories for all vehicles in a nuScenes scene at once, re-planned at 2 Hz in 10 s closed-loop simulations.
Conditioned on
Each vehicle's past states and its agent-centered vector map; relative positions, headings and speeds between vehicle pairs feed the attention layers.
Model
A scene-level diffusion model whose denoiser is a transformer alternating attention over time, between vehicles, and to the map; actions are rolled through unicycle dynamics into states.
Steered by
An LLM writing a loss: GPT-4 turns a plain-English request into a differentiable Python loss, and its gradient guides every denoising step for all vehicles jointly.
Used for
Building AV test scenes from words, such as 'vehicle A should collide with vehicle B' or 'keep within 10–30 m of vehicle B', plus rule-following background traffic.

CTG++ fixes two gaps in CTG. First, CTG planned each car separately, so a follower might not react when its leader slowed; CTG++ denoises all cars in a nuScenes scene together with a transformer that attends across time, across vehicles and to the map. Second, writing rule formulas needs expertise, so the user types a request in plain English. GPT-4, given helper functions and a few request-to-code examples, writes a loss function in Python. During sampling, that loss's gradient nudges every denoising step, as in CTG. Idea worth remembering: the LLM never draws trajectories; it only writes the cost, and the diffusion model keeps the motion realistic.

What they found
  • For 'vehicle A should always keep within 10–30 m of vehicle B', both CTG++ and CTG met the request (violation 0.000), but CTG++ had a failure rate (vehicles crashing or leaving the road) of 0.173 vs 0.343 for CTG (Table 1).
  • Switching the denoiser from agent-centered to scene-centered coordinates raised the failure rate from 0.173 to 0.886 (Table 2).

For mobility: An agency could turn written crash-report narratives into simulated test scenes, letting an LLM write the cost while a trained traffic model supplies realistic motion.

Watch out: GPT-4's loss code is not checked automatically and can mean the wrong thing, complex map-based requests are not supported, and each scenario takes about a minute.

SAFE-SIM

Chang et al. · ECCV 2024 · paper · [P05]
Crashes and near-missesDiffusion
Generates
Short future plans (accelerations and turn rates, rolled out into positions) for every non-AV vehicle, re-planned twice a second in closed loop; one chosen vehicle acts as the adversary.
Conditioned on
Each vehicle's local map image and the recent states of nearby vehicles, starting from real nuScenes scenes (also tested on nuPlan without retraining).
Model
A trajectory diffusion model following CTG: a ResNet encodes the map and history, and a UNet of 1-D temporal convolutions denoises the action sequence in 100 steps.
Steered by
Guidance with cost gradients at every denoising step: approach the AV, hit a set relative speed or time to collision, stay on route, avoid other cars. Partial diffusion starts from a rule-made crash sketch.
Used for
Closed-loop safety testing of AV planners (rule-based, IDM, behavior cloning, BITS, PDM-Closed) against adversaries whose crash type and aggressiveness can be set.

SAFE-SIM replays a real nuScenes scene, but a diffusion model drives the other cars and re-plans as the AV moves. For one chosen car, each denoising step is nudged by the gradient of a cost: get close to the AV, with a chosen relative speed or time to collision. Other costs keep all cars on their routes and apart. To pick a front, side or rear crash, a rule-based sketch of it is partly noised and then denoised, so it keeps its shape but becomes drivable. Idea worth remembering: one trained model gives many tests, changed only by the costs you guide with.

What they found
  • On nuScenes with a rule-based AV planner, the adversary caused a collision in 43.2% of scenes vs 36.4% for STRIVE and 18.2% for DiffScene, with better realism (0.38 vs 0.85 and 0.52; lower is better) (Table 2).
  • Dropping the realism costs raised the adversary's collision rate to 53.5% (from 23.9%) but sent it off the road in 23.1% of cases (from 13.8%) (Table 5).

For mobility: A safety team could turn recorded real scenes into many reactive crash tests, choosing crash type and severity, to stress an automated vehicle's planner before road testing.

Watch out: Realism here is only a match of acceleration and jerk histograms, and some generated crashes are ones the AV could not avoid or was not at fault for.

SoVAR

Guo et al. · ASE 2024 · paper · [N10]
Crashes and near-missesLLM
Generates
Simulator test scenarios (LGSVL with Baidu Apollo): waypoints (x, y, speed) for each crash participant on a chosen road, plus weather and lighting, that replay the reported collision.
Conditioned on
A raw NHTSA crash narrative, and a road picked from the simulator's San Francisco map with its type, length, width and lane count.
Model
The only generative model is GPT-4, used as a reader. Prompts with fixed wording patterns pull out 10 attributes (weather, lanes, speed limit, crash type, each vehicle's actions). It does not write trajectories.
Steered by
Not by a learned model. The Z3 constraint solver finds waypoints that obey the extracted actions, lane directions and speed limit, and makes striker and victim reach the collision area at the same time.
Used for
Testing an automated driving system (Apollo 6.0): each crash participant takes a turn as the self-driving car while the other vehicles replay the solver's paths.

SoVAR rebuilds police-reported crashes inside a driving simulator. GPT-4 reads each NHTSA narrative, guided by prompts that define every attribute and add rules (e.g., skip actions the driver only intended), and returns ten fields such as road type, lane count, crash type and each vehicle's actions. A constraint solver (Z3), not a neural network, then writes the waypoints, fitting the actions to whatever road is chosen and forcing both vehicles to reach the collision area together. Each vehicle then takes a turn as the Apollo-driven car. The lesson: let the LLM read, and let rules guarantee the geometry.

What they found
  • On 150 hand-checked NHTSA reports, GPT-4 with the patterned prompts beat plain GPT-4 by 7.3% and the older rule-based language tool AC3R by 31.9% in average extraction accuracy (Table 3).
  • Tests built from 200 reports led Apollo into 25 collisions, against 4 when the other vehicles followed random paths (Table 6).

For mobility: An agency could turn its own crash narratives into repeatable simulator tests and check whether an automated vehicle avoids the crash types common on its roads.

Watch out: Paths come from hand-written constraints, not learned driving behavior, and GPT-4 extracted pre-crash driving actions correctly in only 76.33% of reports (Table 3).

4 · Rare cases in ADAS and crash data

Add more of the rare scenes and records a model would otherwise ignore.

GAIA-1

Hu et al. · arXiv 2023 · paper · [P22]
Rare cases in ADAS and crash dataToken modelDiffusion
Generates
Driving video at 288×512 pixels and 25 frames per second: continuations of a real clip, or whole scenes made up from scratch, up to minutes long.
Conditioned on
Any mix of: a few seconds of past video, ego speed and curvature over time, and text such as 'It is night' or 'We are 15 meters behind a bus'. Or nothing at all.
Model
An image tokenizer (576 discrete tokens per frame), a 6.5-billion-parameter autoregressive transformer that predicts the next image token, and a 2.6-billion-parameter video diffusion decoder.
Steered by
Conditioning on actions and text, with classifier-free guidance on text (scheduled over tokens and frames) and negative prompts. Top-k = 50 sampling keeps samples varied but realistic.
Used for
Proposed as a neural simulator that makes synthetic and adversarial data for training and validating driving systems; the paper shows capabilities, not a downstream test.

GAIA-1 treats driving video like language. Each frame becomes 576 tokens, and a 6.5-billion-parameter transformer, trained on 4,700 hours of London driving, learns to predict the next token from past frames, text, and the ego car's speed and curvature. Sampling token by token gives one possible future, sampling again gives another (the other car gives way, or not), and a diffusion decoder turns the tokens into smooth video. Because actions are an input, you can command maneuvers the expert data never shows, like drifting out of lane. Idea to remember: a world model is a next-token predictor whose 'words' are scenes.

What they found
  • Commanding left or right steering out of the lane, which never appears in the expert training data, still gave geometrically consistent futures, and in one case an oncoming car swerved to avoid the ego car (Figure 13; examples only, no numbers).
  • The sampling rule matters: always taking the likeliest token made videos repeat, while top-k = 50 sampling gave tokens whose 'surprise' (perplexity) matched real frames (Figure 6).

For mobility: A researcher could replay one real approach to an intersection under different ego maneuvers or weather and see how other road users plausibly react.

Watch out: The evidence is example videos, not measured gains: no test shows the videos improve or validate a driving system, and generation does not yet run in real time.

CTGAN-RU

Chen et al. · arXiv 2024 · paper · [P06]
Rare cases in ADAS and crash dataGAN
Generates
Synthetic fatal-crash records: table rows mixing categories and numbers, such as driver age and sex, drunk or drug driving, collision type, rural or urban, speed limit, curvature and grade.
Conditioned on
A one-hot condition vector that names one category of one discrete variable. Setting crash severity to fatal asks for fatal rows.
Model
Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) with small fully connected generator and discriminator. Numeric columns are coded by Gaussian-mixture modes; the discriminator judges 10 rows at once (PacGAN) to avoid mode collapse.
Steered by
Conditioning: the vector fixes the category, and an extra loss term punishes rows that ignore it. Training picks categories by log-frequency, so rare ones are seen often.
Used for
Rebalancing the training data of a binary logit crash-severity model (fatal vs non-fatal) for Washington State interstate and highway crashes, 2014–2018.

Fatal crashes were only 0.05% of 157,080 Washington highway crashes, so a logit model trained on the raw data predicted no fatal crash correctly. CTGAN-RU first keeps only 114 non-fatal crashes by random under-sampling (RU), then asks a conditional tabular GAN, trained on those plus the 57 real fatal crashes, for rows with severity set to fatal until both classes hold 114. The condition vector is what lets a GAN handle sparse categories like head-on collisions or drug driving. The test set stays real and imbalanced. Idea to remember: generate the rare class on purpose, and judge it on untouched real data.

What they found
  • Share of fatal test crashes caught (sensitivity): 0.875 with CTGAN-RU data, against 0.000 with the raw data, 0.667 with CTGAN alone, 0.583 with SMOTE-NC, 0.458 with TVAE and 0.75 with under-sampling only (Table 4).
  • G-mean, which is high only when both fatal and non-fatal crashes are classified well, was 0.851 for CTGAN-RU, the best of all methods (0.748 CTGAN alone, 0.729 SMOTE-NC, 0.639 TVAE, 0.713 under-sampling; Table 4).

For mobility: A DOT safety analyst could add synthetic fatal or severe crashes with a conditional GAN before fitting a severity model, while always testing on real, untouched records.

Watch out: Only 24 fatal crashes are in the test set, and a logit fit on 1:1 balanced data needs correcting before its probabilities are real-world odds (left to future work).

MagicDrive

Gao et al. · ICLR 2024 · paper · [P02]
Rare cases in ADAS and crash dataDiffusion
Generates
Surround-view camera images of a street scene (the nuScenes camera set) at 224×400 or 272×736 pixels, and short videos in an extension.
Conditioned on
A top-down road map (8 road classes), a 3D box for each object (10 classes), each camera's pose, and a text line such as weather or time of day.
Model
Latent diffusion: pretrained Stable Diffusion v1.5 stays frozen. Only new parts are trained: box and camera encoders (via cross-attention), a ControlNet-style map branch, and attention between neighboring cameras.
Steered by
Conditioning, strengthened at sampling time by classifier-free guidance (scale 2.0 by default). Editing the inputs, such as rotating cars 180° or deleting half the objects, changes the scene.
Used for
Extra labeled training images for camera-based top-down segmentation (CVT) and 3D object detection (BEVFusion). The labels are the boxes and map you fed in.

MagicDrive draws the camera images that should match a labeled 3D scene: a top-down road map, a 3D box for every car or pedestrian, each camera's position, and a sentence such as 'rainy'. It encodes boxes and map separately instead of flattening them into one top-down picture, so object height and distance survive. Pretrained Stable Diffusion does the drawing, and a cross-view attention layer lets each camera look at its left and right neighbors, so a car spanning two images stays one car. Because the scene is fixed first, every image comes with exact labels. Key idea: generate pixels from labels, not labels from pixels.

What they found
  • Training the top-down segmentation model CVT with as many MagicDrive images as real ones raised vehicle mIoU (overlap with the true map) from 36.00 to 40.34 and road mIoU from 74.30 to 79.56; images from BEVGen lowered road mIoU (Table 3).
  • Camera-only 3D detection (BEVFusion) rose from 32.88 to 35.40 mAP, a detection accuracy score, when MagicDrive images were added (Table 2).

For mobility: A researcher could hand-edit box layouts, such as a car turned against traffic or a crowded crossing, and get matching labeled camera images to stress-test a perception model.

Watch out: It cannot create conditions missing from nuScenes: its night images are too bright and requested snow does not appear (Figure 9), so rare weather stays rare.

DriveDreamer

Wang et al. · ECCV 2024 · paper · [P21]
Rare cases in ADAS and crash dataDiffusion
Generates
Driving camera video (single or multi-view) that follows a given road layout, and in the second stage, future video plus the ego car's future driving actions.
Conditioned on
HD-map lines (lane boundaries, dividers, crosswalks) and 3D boxes drawn into the image, a text prompt for weather or time of day, a reference frame, and ego speed and yaw.
Model
Auto-DM, a latent diffusion model built on frozen Stable Diffusion v1.4 with added attention layers. ActionFormer, a transformer with recurrent (GRU) updates, rolls the road layout forward from the actions.
Steered by
Conditioning only: map and boxes enter the denoiser directly, text changes the style (sunny, rainy, night), and a different action sequence (turn left or right) gives a different future video.
Used for
Synthetic training images for 3D object detection, and an open-loop planning check of predicted ego paths on nuScenes.

DriveDreamer learns a 'world model' from 700 nuScenes driving videos. Stage one teaches a diffusion model to draw camera frames that obey a given layout: lane lines, crosswalks and 3D boxes are drawn into the image and fed in with the noise, so cars appear where the boxes say. Stage two adds ActionFormer, which takes the ego car's speed and yaw and predicts how the layout will move; the diffusion model then draws that future. To augment data, the authors took 4K layouts from the training set and rendered new images for them. Idea to remember: learn the traffic structure first, the pixels second.

What they found
  • Adding images rendered from 4K training-set layouts raised BEVFusion's 3D detection score (mAP) from 32.8 to 35.8 (Table 1).
  • Video realism scores (FID 14.9, FVD 340.8) beat the GAN-based DriveGAN (27.8 and 390.8) trained on the same nuScenes data (Table 2, lower is better).

For mobility: A researcher could render the same intersection layout in rain or at night, or under different ego maneuvers, to grow camera training data for rare conditions.

Watch out: The synthetic images redraw layouts already in nuScenes, so they add new looks, not new rare traffic situations; the FCOS3D detector gained only 0.7 mAP (Table 1).

GAIA-2

Russell et al. · arXiv 2025 · paper · [N07]
Rare cases in ADAS and crash dataDiffusion
Generates
Up to five matching surround-camera videos at 448×960 pixels: new scenes from scratch, continuations of real clips, or edits of real video.
Conditioned on
Ego speed and curvature; 3D boxes for other road users; tags for country, weather, time of day, speed limit, lanes, crossings, signals and intersection type; camera geometry; CLIP text or scenario embeddings.
Model
Latent diffusion (trained with flow matching, a close cousin of the usual noise-prediction loss). A video tokenizer compresses frames about 400×, and an 8.4-billion-parameter space-time transformer denoises the latents of all cameras together.
Steered by
Conditioning (actions through adaptive layer norm, the rest through cross-attention). Classifier-free guidance at scale 2 to 20 is switched on only for rare scenes, and only around the conditioned boxes.
Used for
Augmenting driving data (redrawing a real drive in snow or at night) and creating safety-critical cases: unsafe ego steering, or sudden braking and risky crossings by others.

GAIA-2 is GAIA-1's successor, rebuilt as a latent diffusion model over five cameras and trained on about 25 million 2-second clips from the UK, US and Germany. Training mixes three tasks: generate from scratch, continue a real clip, and inpaint a masked region. In use, the same model can sample a new scene, steer it with actions, boxes and road tags, or fill a masked area to insert a car into real video. Partially noising a real clip and denoising it under 'snow' keeps the ego path but changes the weather. Idea to remember: one model, three moves, chosen by what you hold fixed.

What they found
  • Given real starting frames and a rightward-curvature action, the ego car veered into oncoming traffic and the oncoming car swerved away (Figure 9; examples only, no numbers).
  • Realism (FDD, FID), motion consistency (FVMD) and box-placement accuracy (IoU) all improved during training on n = 1024 from-scratch samples, but no other model is compared (Figure 13).

For mobility: A test lab could take one recorded drive and redraw it at night, in rain, or with an added crossing pedestrian to probe a camera-based driving system.

Watch out: Results are mostly example videos and training curves, with no comparison to other models or proof that synthetic clips improve a driver; the data and scenario model are proprietary.

5 · Detector gaps

Fill the holes a failed detector leaves, many times, so the spread shows the uncertainty.

PriSTI

Liu et al. · ICDE 2023 · paper · [P09]
Detector gapsDiffusion
Generates
Values for the missing cells of a sensors × time table (e.g., 5-min speeds from 207 Los Angeles freeway detectors, 24 steps), drawn 100 times to give a median and a 5–95% band.
Conditioned on
The readings that were observed, a quick linear-interpolation fill of the gaps, and a distance-based graph of which sensors are near each other.
Model
Conditional denoising diffusion (DDPM; 50 steps for the traffic data). The noise-predicting network mixes attention over time, attention over sensors and a graph network, with attention weights computed from the interpolated first guess.
Steered by
Nothing beyond the conditions: observed values, the interpolated first guess and the sensor graph guide every denoising step; no cost or guidance term.
Used for
Filling detector gaps (random dropouts, 1–4 hour outages, fully failed sensors) before forecasting or analysis; also tested on Beijing air-quality stations.

PriSTI treats gaps in detector data as a fill-in-the-blank job for a diffusion model. The input is a window of readings from many sensors (e.g., 207 Los Angeles freeway detectors in METR-LA) and a graph of which sensors are close together. First, each sensor's gaps get plain linear interpolation, a noise-free first guess. The diffusion model then starts from random noise in the missing cells only and removes it step by step, using that guess and the graph to decide which times and neighbouring sensors matter. Training hides some real readings and teaches the model to recover them. Idea worth remembering: give the diffusion model a cheap first guess.

What they found
  • With 90% of METR-LA speed readings missing in long blocks, PriSTI's mean absolute error was 4.67%-34.11% lower than the three best baselines: BRITS, GRIN and CSDI, an earlier diffusion imputer (Fig. 5).
  • A forecaster (Graph WaveNet) trained on PriSTI-filled Beijing air-quality data reached MAE 29.34, vs 36.97 on the raw gappy data and 30.20 with CSDI filling (Table V).

For mobility: An agency could fill outages in loop-detector or PeMS-style speed data and keep an uncertainty band for every filled value, instead of one silent guess.

Watch out: On the traffic datasets the gaps were injected artificially (random points or blocks), so test it on your own real outage patterns before trusting the filled values.

DiffSTG

Wen et al. · ACM SIGSPATIAL 2023 · paper · [P23]
Detector gapsDiffusion
Generates
Traffic flow at every detector for the next 12 five-minute steps, as several samples (8 in the tests); their spread is the uncertainty and their average is the point forecast.
Conditioned on
The past 12 steps at all detectors (future cells masked out) and the road graph, where two sensors are linked if they are on the same road.
Model
Conditional denoising diffusion (DDPM). The denoiser, UGnet, is a U-shaped stack of time convolutions at several time scales plus graph convolutions between sensors.
Steered by
Nothing beyond the conditions: it samples futures that fit the visible history and the graph. Skipping denoising steps makes sampling faster.
Used for
Probabilistic traffic-flow forecasting on PeMS freeway detectors (PEMS08, 170 sensors); also PM2.5 forecasting at air-quality stations in Beijing and Guangzhou.

DiffSTG forecasts detector traffic as a range of possible futures, not one line. It puts the last 12 and the next 12 five-minute flows from 170 PeMS detectors into one block, hides the future part, and asks a diffusion model to fill it. Starting from random noise, a denoising network called UGnet removes noise step by step, looking at the visible history and the road graph linking neighbouring sensors; it mixes time convolutions at several time scales with graph convolutions across sensors. Eight runs give eight futures; their spread is the forecast band. Idea worth remembering: a forecast is gap filling where the gap is the future.

What they found
  • On CRPS, a score of how well the whole forecast range fits what happened (lower is better), DiffSTG beat the best other probabilistic method by 14.3% on PEMS08 traffic flow and by 5.6% and 4.3% on the two air-quality sets (Table 2).
  • Generating all 12 future steps in one denoising run made it about 40× faster than TimeGrad, an earlier diffusion forecaster that produces one step at a time (Table 3).

For mobility: A traffic management center could publish detector forecasts with a likely range and plan staffing or ramp metering for the high end, not only the average.

Watch out: Its average forecast is still less accurate than the best deterministic graph models (Table 5); what you gain is the uncertainty band, not a sharper single number.

6 · Digital twins and simulated worlds

Fill in a whole road and its traffic from partial views, then run it forward.

UniSim

Yang et al. · CVPR 2023 · paper · [N04]
Digital twins and simulated worldsNeural field
Generates
Camera images and lidar point clouds of a recorded street seen from new positions, with vehicles moved, removed or added (e.g., the test car shifted 2–3 m sideways).
Conditioned on
One recorded drive (front camera + 360° lidar, 8-s PandaSet clips), vehicle boxes and tracks, and the new scene layout and sensor position you choose.
Model
Mostly reconstruction: neural feature fields (background voxel grid, one field per vehicle), volume rendering and a CNN decoder. Generative parts: a latent-code vehicle shape prior and an adversarial (GAN) loss.
Steered by
Not steered toward a goal: you edit the scene by hand (move cars, change the test car's path) and it re-renders; the adversarial loss pushes unseen views to look real.
Used for
Closed-loop testing of a self-driving stack on edited safety-critical scenes (cut-ins, oncoming car) and extra training views for camera-based vehicle detection.

UniSim turns one recorded drive into an editable 3D copy of the street, a digital twin. Background and moving vehicles are stored separately as neural fields: learned 3D grids saying what surface and colour sit at each point. It then places vehicles where you want, traces camera and lidar rays through the scene and renders images and point clouds. Most of this is fitting and rendering, not generating. The generative pieces fill what was never seen: a shared shape prior completes hidden sides of cars, and an adversarial loss makes off-path views look real. Idea worth remembering: separate background from vehicles so you can edit the scene.

What they found
  • Training a camera-based vehicle detector on real logs plus UniSim-rendered extra viewpoints gave mAP 42.9; adding views from the FVS or Instant-NGP renderers instead gave 41.1 or 40.1 (Table 5).
  • For views shifted 2 m and 3 m sideways, where no real photo exists, UniSim's realism score (FID, lower is better) was 74.7 and 97.5, the best of the four renderers compared (Table 1).

For mobility: An AV tester or agency could replay a logged near-miss, then move the other car or shift the test vehicle's path, and see how the automated driver reacts.

Watch out: Realism drops as views move further from the recorded path (worse at 3 m than 2 m), and each twin fits one log; it cannot invent a new street.

TrafficBots

Zhang et al. · ICRA 2023 · paper · [P20]
Digital twins and simulated worldsVAE
Generates
Next-step actions (acceleration, yaw rate) and positions for every vehicle, cyclist and pedestrian around the test car, rolled out in 0.1 s steps for 80 future steps.
Conditioned on
Shared map, traffic-light states and all agents' current states, plus each agent's own destination (a map polyline) and personality code.
Model
Conditional VAE: a 16-number Gaussian 'personality' latent per agent, fixed for the whole run, feeds one shared transformer + GRU driving policy; a unicycle model turns actions into motion.
Steered by
Choice of destination and personality: sampling them gives different futures (6 per scene for motion prediction). No cost-based guidance.
Used for
Reactive background traffic (bots) for testing AV planning modules, and multi-agent motion prediction on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset.

TrafficBots is a learned 'bot' driver for every road user around the test car, so background traffic reacts instead of replaying a recording. Each agent gets two private inputs: a destination (where it is heading) and a personality, a 16-number code learned with a conditional VAE that captures driving style. All agents share one policy network that reads the map, traffic lights and nearby agents and outputs acceleration and yaw rate; a simple vehicle model moves everyone 0.1 s forward, then the loop repeats. Sampling other personalities and destinations gives other plausible futures. Idea worth remembering: keep each agent's latent fixed for the run so it means one driving style.

What they found
  • Removing the personality latent cut motion-prediction mAP from 0.18 to 0.06 and raised the average position gap when replaying logged scenes from 0.80 m to 1.29 m (Table II).
  • Plain behaviour cloning without personality or destination (a SimNet-style baseline) had 21.9% of vehicles colliding vs 11.5% for TrafficBots (Table II).

For mobility: A simulation team could fill AV test scenes with reactive, human-like bots whose driving style varies by sampled personality, instead of log replay or hand-tuned car-following rules.

Watch out: As a motion predictor it trails open-loop methods (Table I), and 11.5% of simulated vehicles still collided, so bots are not yet a safe stand-in for human drivers.

SceneDiffuser++

Tan et al. · CVPR 2025 · paper · [P07]
Digital twins and simulated worldsDiffusion
Generates
The whole traffic scene over time: each agent's position, heading, size, type and an on/off 'validity' flag, plus traffic-light positions and states, rolled out for 60 s and longer.
Conditioned on
The road map, the scene history, and the test vehicle's moves from a separate planner; inpainting masks say which cells are known and which to generate.
Model
One diffusion model (SceneDiffuser's axial-attention transformer denoiser) over a 'multi-tensor' of agents × time × features and lights × time × features, trained with a single denoising loss.
Steered by
Inpainting masks only (known history and controlled agents stay fixed); no cost guidance. A 'soft clipping' step during denoising keeps the sparse on/off channel stable.
Used for
Trip-level, point A-to-B closed-loop simulation for testing an automated vehicle's planner, on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset with maps enlarged to a 1 km radius.

SceneDiffuser++ is a traffic world model: given a map and the recent past, it generates what every other road user and traffic light does next. The scene is a table (agents × time × features), and the model fills the future cells by denoising, like inpainting a picture. The new piece is an on/off 'validity' channel per agent and time step: generating it lets the model decide when cars appear, hide behind others, reappear or leave, so traffic keeps flowing on new streets. It trains on 9.1-second Waymo clips yet rolls forward for minutes. Idea worth remembering: one on/off channel turns a fixed cast of cars into a living city.

What they found
  • With an IDM-driven test car, the overall gap between simulated and logged traffic statistics over 60 s (composite JS divergence, lower is better) was 0.2878 with SceneDiffuser++ as the world model vs 0.4793 for IDM rules and 0.4797 for the original SceneDiffuser (Table 1).
  • Collision and off-road realism were worse than with IDM or SceneDiffuser, partly because new cars can be spawned onto the planner's route and many are placed in parking lots (Table 1, Sec. 4.2).

For mobility: An agency or AV tester could run long point-to-point simulated trips where cars enter, leave and obey signals, to compare trip travel times and safety rates.

Watch out: Realism falls as rollouts get longer (30 s to 300 s, Table 2), and 'realistic' here means matching logged statistics, not that each simulated trip is safe.

DriveArena

Yang et al. · ICCV 2025 · paper · [P08]
Digital twins and simulated worldsDiffusion
Generates
Surround-view (multi-camera) street images, frame after frame, matching the simulated road layout and vehicle positions, in a style set by a text prompt such as 'downtown, daytime, cloudy'.
Conditioned on
Map and vehicle boxes from the traffic simulator, drawn into each camera view; a text prompt; camera parameters; the previous generated frame and ego motion as a reference.
Model
World Dreamer: Stable Diffusion v1.5 with ControlNet for layout control, cross-view attention for consistency between cameras, and frame-by-frame autoregressive generation; trained on nuScenes.
Steered by
Conditioning only (layouts, text, reference image). Vehicle motion is not generated: a rule-based traffic simulator (LimSim) moves all background cars and checks collisions.
Used for
Open- and closed-loop testing of camera-based end-to-end driving agents (UniAD, VAD) on four routes in Boston and Singapore.

DriveArena splits a driving simulator into two jobs. A conventional traffic simulator, LimSim, handles motion: it loads a road network from OpenStreetMap, moves all background cars and checks for crashes. The generative part, World Dreamer, handles appearance: a diffusion model turns each simulator snapshot (map and vehicle boxes drawn into each camera view) into realistic camera images, using the previous frame as a reference so the video stays consistent. The driving agent sees only those images and outputs a path; the simulator moves the ego car along it, and the loop repeats. Idea worth remembering: a simulator handles motion, a generative model handles what cameras see.

What they found
  • Swapping real nuScenes images for World Dreamer images of the same drives barely changed UniAD's open-loop driving score (PDMS, 0 to 1): 0.902 vs 0.91 (Table 2).
  • In closed loop, two published driving agents completed only 4.59% (VAD) and 13.7% (UniAD) of the routes on average, mostly failing at the first intersection turn, which open-loop scores had hidden (Table 3).

For mobility: A DOT or AV testing program could test camera-based driving software on its own local streets, downloaded from OpenStreetMap, without building a 3D model of the city.

Watch out: Generated images still lose a lot for perception (3D detection on them scores far below real images, Table 1), so passing in DriveArena is not passing on the road.

PMA-Diffusion

Liu, Jin & Choi · Transportation Research Part C 2026 · paper · [N03]
Digital twins and simulated worldsDiffusion
Generates
A full time-space speed map of an I-24 corridor near Nashville: 200 × 200 cells of 100 ft × 1 s (about 3.8 miles × 200 s); repeated runs give an ensemble.
Conditioned on
Only the observed cells: fixed loop-detector rows (5–25% of rows) plus the cells crossed by sampled probe-vehicle trajectories.
Model
Unconditional diffusion prior (UNet denoiser, 500 steps) trained only on masked, incomplete speed maps, then used inside a RePaint-style inpainting sampler.
Steered by
At each denoising step the observed cells are reset to their measured values, then an adaptive smoothing step nudges the missing cells along free-flow and congested wave directions.
Used for
Highway traffic state estimation: rebuilding speed maps, including stop-and-go waves, from sparse loop-detector and probe-vehicle data.

PMA-Diffusion treats traffic state estimation as filling in a time-space speed map. Stage 1 teaches a diffusion model what highway speed maps look like from sparse, masked maps only, since complete ground truth is rare; a 'double mask' hides extra cells in training so even always-observed detector rows get practised. Stage 2 estimates a new map: start from noise and denoise; after every step, paste the measured cells back in, then smooth the missing cells along free-flow and congested wave directions, as in adaptive smoothing. Tests mask I-24 MOTION camera data to mimic loops and probes. Idea worth remembering: physics enters at sampling time, so one prior serves any sensor layout.

What they found
  • With a prior trained on complete maps, 5% of rows observed and no probes, the error on hidden cells (Masked-MSE) was 0.1463 for physics smoothing alone, 0.0172 with diffusion inpainting (RePaint) and 0.0167 with PMA's physics step added (Table 2, Fig. 6).
  • Trained on sparse data only, in that same sparsest case the double-mask prior reached 0.0289 vs 0.0364 for the plain single-mask prior, closing part of the gap to the complete-data prior (Table 2).

For mobility: An agency with loop detectors and a few percent of probe vehicles could rebuild corridor speed maps, including stop-and-go waves, and reuse the same model when detectors change.

Watch out: Ground truth came from I-24 MOTION camera data masked on purpose; real loop and GPS data add bias and time delay that the authors assumed away.

7 · Lidar from a camera

Generate the scan a second sensor would have seen, and learn what it cannot add.

LiDM

Ran, Guizilini & Wang · CVPR 2024 · paper · [N05]
Lidar from a cameraDiffusion
Generates
Full 360° lidar sweeps stored as range images (64 × 1024 for 64-beam KITTI-360, 32 × 1024 for 32-beam nuScenes), which convert back to 3D point clouds without loss.
Conditioned on
Nothing (unconditional), a semantic map (SemanticKITTI), a front camera image (KITTI-360), or a text prompt (zero-shot, through CLIP's shared text–image space).
Model
Latent diffusion. A lidar-tailored autoencoder (reconstruction, adversarial and vector-quantization losses) compresses the range image; a U-Net diffusion model denoises the latent; the decoder turns it back into a scan.
Steered by
Conditioning only. Semantic maps enter as an image-to-image input; camera views become CLIP feature vectors passed to the denoiser through a condition encoder; text reuses that CLIP space.
Used for
Realistic synthetic lidar for autonomous-driving perception and simulation, made from cheaper inputs such as semantic labels, camera images or a sentence.

LiDM stores each lidar sweep as a range image: a 2D grid where each row is one laser beam and each pixel holds a distance. An autoencoder squeezes this grid into a small latent grid, built around how lidar works: it compresses only along each beam's scan line so the ring-shaped curves survive, it checks the decoded 3D point positions, and it adds patch blocks for large nearby objects. A latent diffusion model then learns to denoise in this space. A semantic map, camera views or a text prompt steer the denoising. Idea to remember: realism comes mainly from a sensor-aware latent space, not from a bigger diffusion model.

What they found
  • Unconditional 64-beam scenes in 50 steps: 20.4% better FRID and 31.0% better FPVD (realism distances, lower is better) than plain Latent Diffusion with the same steps (Table 1).
  • Speed: 1.603 scans/sec vs 0.015 for LiDARGen, a diffusion model working on the full-size range image, about ×107 faster on one RTX 3090 (Fig. 1, Table 3).

For mobility: A researcher with camera-only probe vehicles could create lidar-like scans to test 3D perception, after checking them against real lidar from similar roads.

Watch out: Camera-to-LiDAR only conditions the area the camera sees; the rest is generated freely, and the authors note a generated car 'still struggles with its precise scale in 3D space'.

Veila

Liu et al. · arXiv 2025 · paper · [N06]
Lidar from a cameraDiffusion
Generates
A full 360° lidar scan as a range image (depth and return intensity per pixel), including the rear half that the camera never sees.
Conditioned on
One front-camera RGB image plus the camera calibration matrices (K, T); a three-camera version is also tested on nuScenes.
Model
A DDPM-style diffusion model whose U-Net predicts the noise on the range image directly. Three add-on modules inside the U-Net handle camera features, camera–lidar alignment and panorama-wide consistency.
Steered by
Conditioning only: semantic and depth features from two frozen image networks, weighted by a learned confidence, enter by cross-attention along each lidar ray; a global self-attention layer spreads them to unseen areas.
Used for
Extra training scans for lidar semantic segmentation when labels are scarce, lidar scenes for fog, snow and night, and scene editing (removing or replacing objects).

You give Veila one front-camera photo; it returns a 360° lidar scan, stored as a range image: a 2D grid where each pixel holds the distance and strength of one laser return. A diffusion model denoises this grid step by step. At each step it reads the photo through two frozen networks, one for objects and one for depth, trusting whichever is more reliable in each spot. Each lidar ray has a fixed direction, so the calibration tells which photo pixels lie along it, even while the scan is still noise. Global attention carries this to the rear half. Idea to remember: align sensors with known geometry, not the noisy sample.

What they found
  • SemanticKITTI: FRD 220.40 and FPD 8.18 (realism distances, lower is better) vs 262.85 and 12.06 for R2DM, an unconditional range-image diffusion model (Table 1).
  • Added as training data with only 1% of SemanticKITTI labels, Veila scans raise MinkUNet segmentation mIoU by +1.6 over scans from R2DM (Table 5).

For mobility: A researcher could turn ordinary dashcam images, including night, fog or snow, into extra lidar training scans for 3D perception, once the model is trained on paired camera–lidar data.

Watch out: The rear half of each scan has no camera evidence behind it, and the fog, snow and night test set (KITTI-Weather) is itself built from synthetic images and simulated lidar.

8 · Storm and road damage

Paint damage onto roads you already have, with the mask as a free label.

Kalluri et al.

Kalluri et al. · CVPR 2024 Workshops · paper · [N09]
Storm and road damageToken model
Generates
Synthetic post-disaster aerial images: the building at the center of a real pre-disaster image redrawn as damaged or intact, each labeled by its prompt.
Conditioned on
A real pre-disaster image from the new region, a center mask (shifted slightly at random), and a prompt from a damaged or undamaged prompt pool for the disaster type.
Model
MUSE, a pretrained masked-token transformer (not diffusion): VQGAN turns the image into discrete tokens, the transformer fills the masked tokens in parallel, VQGAN decodes them. Used frozen or adapter-fine-tuned.
Steered by
The text prompt and the mask; four images are made per image–prompt pair and the one with the highest CLIP image–text similarity is kept.
Used for
Training a pre/post-disaster building damage classifier (siamese ViT) for a region with no post-disaster labels: pretrain on other disasters, then retrain only the last layer on synthetic pairs.

After a disaster you usually have satellite images from before, but no labeled after images. This paper makes them. It masks a patch at the center of each before image, where the building is, and asks MUSE, a text-to-image model, to refill it from a prompt such as 'a bird's-eye view of a building destroyed by a hurricane' or 'a house under tree shade'. The prompt sets the label, so no one annotates. A damage classifier is first trained on real labeled pairs from other disasters, then only its last layer is retrained on the synthetic pairs. Idea to remember: edit real before-images instead of generating whole scenes.

What they found
  • xBD, trained on the other disasters: AUPRC (area under the precision–recall curve) 54.40 with synthetic target images vs 25.27 without them (Fig. 1, Table 3).
  • The gain is much smaller across US hurricanes (SKAI): a 5.33% improvement over the source-only baseline in the same setting (Table 3).

For mobility: After a hurricane, an agency with only pre-storm imagery of a new county could build a first damage classifier for it, then check it on the first real post-storm images.

Watch out: Labels come from the prompt, not from checking the picture; the authors note training is sensitive to low-quality generated images, so a bad edit becomes a wrong label.

RoadFusion

Aqeel, Bellete & Setti · ICIAP 2025 · paper · [N08]
Storm and road damageDiffusion
Generates
Pavement images with a synthetic defect (crack, pothole, raveling, patch damage) painted into a chosen region of an otherwise clean road photo.
Conditioned on
A defect-free pavement image, a text description of the defect, a negative prompt, and a binary mask marking where the defect may appear.
Model
A latent diffusion model (DIAG) doing mask-based inpainting, used only at training time. Detection itself uses a WideResNet-50 feature extractor, two small adapters and a two-layer discriminator.
Steered by
The text prompt and negative prompt choose the defect type; the mask fixes its location. Nothing beyond these conditions.
Used for
Training a pixel-level pavement defect detector (crack and pothole heat maps) when few labeled defect images exist; at test time only the real-image path runs.

RoadFusion learns what normal pavement looks like and flags the rest as defects. Defect photos are scarce, so the authors take clean road photos, draw a mask where a defect could be, and ask a latent diffusion model to paint a crack or pothole there from a text prompt. Features of real clean images and of these synthetic defect images pass through two separate adapters, and a small network learns to score each patch as normal or defective. At test time the generator is switched off and the detector outputs a defect heat map. Idea to remember: the generator only supplies the rare class; real data covers the common one.

What they found
  • EDM Crack (fine cracks, Edmonton roads): IoU (overlap between predicted and true defect pixels) 0.72 vs 0.67 for the best earlier method (Table 1).

For mobility: A city or DOT with many clean pavement photos but few labeled cracks could paint realistic defects onto them to train a crack and pothole mapping model.

Watch out: The paper reports no run without the synthetic defects, so you cannot tell how much the diffusion model itself helps; each dataset has only one or two comparison methods.

Surveys

Where to look for more, and how others organize the field.

Synthetic mobility review

Kapp, Hansmeyer & Mihaljević · arXiv 2024 · paper · [P13]
SurveysSurvey
Generates
Nothing itself. It reviews 51 papers (2012–2023) that generate synthetic trajectories of people in cities: single trips (e.g., taxi rides), one person's stops over days, or a whole city population.
Conditioned on
The reviewed models learn from GPS traces, phone call records, transit smart-card taps, social-media check-ins or travel surveys; some add road networks or census data.
Model
Markov chains and fitted distributions, LSTMs, GANs, VAEs and inverse reinforcement learning; deep learning appears from 2017. No diffusion models are covered (the search ended in March 2023).
Steered by
Not applicable (a review). It sorts models by the kind of mobility they target and by privacy protection, mostly differential privacy: adding calibrated noise so no single person changes the output much.
Used for
Choosing a synthesis method for a given dataset and purpose: open data release, internal sharing, software testing, or training models such as next-location prediction.

The review asks three questions a data owner would ask: does a method fit my data, how does it work, and does it give enough privacy and enough utility (how well the synthetic data match the real data)? It groups the 51 models into single trips, user movements and city population. It then lists which statistics each paper checks, such as trip length, visits per location, OD flows or how far each person ranges, and with which distance measure. Its main finding: papers measure success in different ways, so results are hard to compare. Idea worth remembering: say which statistics must survive, and at what grid size, before choosing a model.

What they found
  • 43 of the 51 reviewed papers give privacy as a reason to make synthetic data, yet only around half give a formal privacy guarantee or test privacy (Section 4.3).
  • Only eight of the 51 papers check whether the synthetic data reproduce OD flows (Section 4.4.1, Table 2).

For mobility: Before an agency releases or buys synthetic trip data, it can use this review's checklist: name the use, the statistics that must match, and the privacy test.

Watch out: Utility depends on grid size (a model can match a 2 km grid well and a 250 m grid poorly), and differential privacy protects individuals, not groups.

Diffusion models in ITS (survey)

Peng et al. · arXiv 2024 · paper · [P29]
SurveysSurvey
Generates
Covers diffusion models that generate trajectories, driving images and video, point clouds, traffic flow on spatio-temporal graphs, GPS trajectories, and accident videos from text.
Conditioned on
Groups conditions into sensor features (lidar, camera), spatial features (road network, BEV, layouts), temporal inputs (past tracks, departure times) and semantic ones (text, intents, traffic rules as logic formulas).
Model
Explains DDPM, score-based and SDE views, then conditional and latent diffusion; Table I lists each reviewed model's task, condition, architecture, datasets and code.
Steered by
Compares four ways in (Fig. 2): concatenation, cross-attention, classifier guidance (e.g., cost functions, reinforcement learning) and classifier-free guidance.
Used for
Four ITS areas: autonomous driving, traffic simulation, traffic forecasting and traffic safety, plus future directions such as pairing LLMs with diffusion and faster sampling.

This survey is a map of diffusion models in transportation, written from the ITS side. It first explains the forward (add noise) and reverse (remove noise) processes, then the two variants you will meet most: conditional diffusion, where history, maps or text steer the output, and latent diffusion, which denoises a compressed version of the data to save time. It then walks through four application areas, arranged as in Fig. 6, and Table I in the appendix lists every reviewed model with its task, condition, architecture, datasets and code. Read Section II-B and Fig. 2: the four ways a condition enters the model are the toolbox behind the 'steer' move.

What they found
  • Conditioning trade-off: cross-attention handles text and other multi-modal conditions but does not offer control over the strength of the condition; classifier and classifier-free guidance add that control, at the cost of a classifier or extra training (Sec. II-B).
  • Speed is the main barrier for real-time ITS and edge devices: computational cost and slow sampling 'remain major bottlenecks' (Sec. V-E).

For mobility: A transportation researcher can use Table I to find a diffusion model, dataset and open code already matched to their task, such as trajectory, traffic flow or GPS data generation.

Watch out: It is a catalog, not a benchmark: models are not compared on common data, and claimed advantages such as privacy and rare-event coverage are argued, not measured.

Foundation models for scenarios (survey)

Gao et al. · IEEE Open Journal of ITS 2026 · paper · [P30]
SurveysSurvey
Generates
