Covers models that generate driving scenarios: agent trajectories and traffic flow, road layouts and starting positions, street-view images, multi-camera driving videos, and safety-critical cases.
Conditioned on
Text prompts, sensor data, maps and road topology, initial agent states, bounding boxes, BEV sketches, control actions and human feedback.
Model
Five families: large language models, vision-language models, multimodal LLMs, diffusion models (Section VI, Table 8) and world models (Section VII); also datasets, simulators, metrics and benchmark challenges.
Steered by
For diffusion traffic generators it names three routes: gradient-based guidance (traffic rules, collision objectives), architecture conditioning (tokens, masks, inpainting) and preference optimization; an LLM can write the guidance function.
Used for
Scenario-based testing of automated vehicles: creating diverse, controllable, safety-critical scenarios, and analyzing scenarios for risk and behavior.

This survey asks how large pretrained models help create and judge test scenarios for automated vehicles. Generation means making diverse, safety-critical, controllable situations; analysis means rating scenarios for risk or behavior. It reviews papers from October 2022 to May 2025 across five model families. Section VI is the one for this course: it sorts diffusion work by output (traffic flow, static road elements, images, videos), and Table 8 lists each model's inputs, the factors you can control (speed, traffic density, weather) and whether it targets safety-critical cases. Sections IX and X list open problems. Remember the split: a model that writes scenarios does not prove they are realistic.

What they found
  • Scope: 345 papers, of which 93 on scenario generation, 56 on scenario analysis, 57 on datasets, 21 on simulators and 25 on benchmark challenges (Table 1).
  • Diffusion generators often score well on statistical realism metrics, yet their trajectories and scenes frequently lack fine-grained physical plausibility, such as vehicles that defy inertia (Sec. VI).

For mobility: A safety researcher can use Table 8 to pick a diffusion scenario generator whose inputs and controllable factors (speed, traffic density, weather) match their test plan.

Watch out: The authors note there is no standard metric yet for realism, controllability or safety-criticality, so results across the reviewed papers are not directly comparable.

What the papers share

Put the papers side by side and most of them follow one recipe.

  1. Learn from a lot of ordinary data. Normal driving logs, months of detector speeds, taxi GPS traces, clean road images. The rare event you care about is almost never what trains the model.
  2. Say what you want with a condition. A map and past tracks, 3D boxes and a weather word, a mask over the missing part, a camera image, or a sentence.
  3. Push harder when a condition is not enough. Add a cost and nudge every denoising step toward it (guidance), search the latent space of a VAE for the output you want, or let a language model write the cost.
  4. Hand the samples to a downstream task (a planner under test, a detector in training, a travel-time report) and judge the generator by that task, not by how real the samples look.

Which model family for which job

FamilyWhat it does well hereSeen inWatch for
VAEFast sampling, and a latent space you can search or optimize inTrajectron++, STRIVE, TrafficBotsAveraged, blurry outputs; latent dimensions are not causes
GANOne-shot sampling; mixed numeric and categorical recordsSocial GAN, CTGAN-RUMode collapse: only the common cases come out
DiffusionHigh-quality samples that are easy to condition, guide, and inpaintMotionDiffuser, CTG, SAFE-SIM, PriSTI, DiffTraj, MagicDrive, LiDM, PMA-Diffusion, and most papers after 2023Many denoising steps make it slow; strong guidance can produce impossible behavior
Token modelLong rollouts and joint futures, with the same machinery as a language model (next token, or masked tokens filled in parallel)MotionLM, GAIA-1, TrafficGen; MUSE in Kalluri et al.Errors compound over long rollouts; the token grid limits precision
LLM front endTurns a sentence or a crash report into a structured scene or a costLCTGen, CTG++, SoVARThe language model can misread the request; check its structured output
Neural fieldRebuilds a recorded scene so it can be rendered from new viewpointsUniSimMostly reconstruction, not invention: it cannot show what no camera saw

How the practice moved

2018–2020: GANs and conditional VAEs draw several futures for pedestrians and vehicles (Social GAN, Trajectron++). 2022–2023: diffusion takes over. Guided diffusion controls simulated traffic (CTG, MotionDiffuser), fills sensor gaps (PriSTI, DiffSTG), and makes synthetic GPS trips and OD tables (DiffTraj, DiffODGen). VAE latent search finds crash scenarios (STRIVE). Language arrives as a front end (LCTGen, CTG++), and driving video gets its first world models (GAIA-1, DriveDreamer). 2024–2026: closed loops and whole worlds (SAFE-SIM, SceneDiffuser++, DriveArena, GAIA-2), one sensor generated from another (LiDM, Veila), physics-guided traffic state estimation (PMA-Diffusion), and synthetic damage for small datasets (Kalluri et al., RoadFusion).

Check yourself

1. You must test an AV planner on unprotected left turns, and later report a crash rate to a state DOT. Which papers do you read first, and what must you add?

SAFE-SIM or CTG, to steer a model of normal driving toward dangerous left turns. But steering changes how often each event appears, so the share of collisions in steered tests is not a crash rate. Add importance-sampling weights, as in Feng et al. (listed under “Read alongside”), or report rates only from naturalistic exposure.

2. A county has 40 labeled photos of washouts and 20,000 FL511 frames of clean roads. Which papers fit, and what is the cheapest baseline?

Kalluri et al. (mask-based editing of real images) and RoadFusion (defects controlled by text and masks). The cheapest baseline is copy-paste: cut real damage out of the 40 photos and paste it onto clean roads. Test on a storm the model never saw.

3. A paper shows its generated driving videos look more realistic than a rival’s. Why is that not enough for an ADAS team?

Realism scores measure appearance. The team needs to know whether training on the generated data improves a detector or planner on real held-out data, whether the objects match their labels, and whether the rare cases they need actually appear. MagicDrive is a good example of reporting the downstream test.

Read alongside (not generative models)

  • Feng et al. (2021), NADE, Nature Communications, and Feng et al. (2023), D2RL, Nature: how to keep a crash-rate estimate unbiased when tests are steered toward danger. NADE · D2RL
  • Wang et al. (2019), Pseudo-LiDAR, CVPR: the classical baseline for lidar from a camera. arXiv:1812.07179
  • Ghiasi et al. (2021), Simple Copy-Paste, CVPR: the cheap baseline for damage augmentation. arXiv:2012.07177
  • Treiber & Helbing (2002), adaptive smoothing method: the classical baseline for filling a speed field from sparse data. arXiv:cond-mat/0210050
  • TrafficGPT, Open-TI, LLMLight and CoLLMLight are language-model agents rather than generators of traffic data; they are read with the AI agents unit in Module 5.
